newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE - Gulf arms bazaar seen thriving in short term.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gulf arms bazaar seen thriving in short term.

text.p: In the early morning hours of a blistering August day in 1990, the might of Iraqi armour steamrolled into tiny Kuwait.
Iraqi forces hardened by an eight-year war with Iran swallowed one of the world's smallest but wealthiest states.
The rumbling of Iraqi tanks sent shock waves through Kuwait's Gulf Arab allies -- sparsely populated countries with vast oil wealth but not enough military firepower to protect it.

Haunted by memories of the lightning Iraqi invasion, Gulf Arab states have pumped billions of petrodollars into high-tech weapons, and everyone from Western arms makers to middlemen has cashed in on their security jitters.
Lingering fears of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and deep suspicions of regional power Iran continue to fuel the thriving Gulf arms bazaar.
Saudi Arabia alone signed arms transfer deals worth $75.9 billion in the 1987-1994 period and has a variety of U.S. arms on order worth $25 billion until the end of the century.

"Most defence ministries across the world have shrinking budgets," said Abu Dhabi-based Jean-Bernard Vialle, Giat Industries' branch executive director. "The GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) market is not saturated and it will not be for several years.
"The Americans always point out the danger of Iraq and Iran. This adds to the thrill of Gulf states buying more weapons."
From political maverick Qatar to oil giant and key U.S. ally Saudi Arabia, Gulf Arab states will keep pouring billions of dollars into arms purchases in the next few years, industry executives say.
ARMS SELLERS ARE FIERCE RIVALS

The United States, France and Britain are in fierce rivalry to grab market share -- with promises of protection and intense lobbying in high-level meetings and lavish entertaining at arms shows where big deals are often announced.
The latest deal -- an $825 million package to supply Qatar with armoured personnel carriers, patrol boats, training aircraft and missiles -- went to Britain.

But industry analysts say the United States has gained an edge in the region after leading the 1991 Gulf War to liberate Kuwait. And France's aggressive lobbying has given it major slices of the market.

It is difficult to estimate how much money Gulf Arab states have channelled into arms purchases in the last six years, but past deals and hefty packages on the horizon provide a window on the scope of the market.
Regional heavyweight Saudi Arabia is seen as the leading customer, despite recent cuts.
"It will always be Saudi Arabia. It is the biggest procurer and it has the longest borders," said a Western diplomat.
Defence Minister Prince Sultan has said the country would boost its armed forces with men and equipment in its next five-year military plan starting in 1997.
One industry executive estimates that Saudi Arabia has spent about $4 billion on new procurements and $800 million on Patriot missiles since the Gulf War.
France is Riyadh's third-biggest arms supplier after the United States and Britain, with weapons sales averaging $1.2 billion a year.
BIG BUYERS ARE SAUDI, KUWAIT AND UAE

Kuwait is also a leading customer. Its defence ministry was allocated 460 million dinars ($1.38 billion) but the funds do not include the country's arms procurement programme worth $12 billion in the 1992-2004 period.
"Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates are the biggest markets. But the UAE has emerged as an important player," said the industry executive.

In the quiet UAE capital of Abu Dhabi, behind the closed doors of sheikhs' palaces, arms executives offer their high-tech weapons and Western government officials offer to come to the UAE's rescue in the event of Iranian aggression.
And everybody from middlemen to technical experts gets in on the wheeling and dealing.
"It's a very complicated process," said the Western diplomat. "By the time the decision reaches the top sheikhs, a lot of middlemen -- Americans, British, Lebanese and others -- make a lot of money."

Abu Dhabi, nervously watching non-Arab Iran across the waterway, has spent huge sums on everything from main battle tanks to fast patrol boats, and the last contract of its size this century is in the pipeline.
Western firms are competing to sell the UAE up to 80 long-range strike aircraft worth up to $6 billion. Lockheed Martin Corp of the United States and France's Dassault Aviation are remaining bidders.
And there are possibilities not far away in Doha. Qatar and foreign companies are pumping more than $10 billion into gas projects that will yield big cash.

"Qatar is up and coming. As they get their gas on line they will become quite well off, probably one of the wealthiest Gulf countries. They will catch up in time with defence procurement," said the industry executive.
